10.0.0.en: It mentions Nehemiah and the chief priests who sealed, twenty-two in number, although the chief priests number twenty-four, as the prophet David arranged. Perhaps two of the chief priests were prevented by circumstances of illness from being present and taking part in sealing the covenant. The priests sealed first, after Nehemiah, to be an example to those after them.

10.1.0.en: It mentions the heads of the Levites who sealed the covenant, 17 in number. Their order comes after the priests in the covenant because they are helpers of the priests in the service of the house of the Lord and are responsible with them for teaching the people. Most of these Levites taught the people and explained the book of the Law (ch. 9:4-5).

10.2.0.en: After the Levites, the leaders of the people came forward, forty-four in number, and sealed the covenant, declaring their responsibility for leading the people in holding fast to the terms of this covenant. Most of these leaders were mentioned in (ch. 7:8). The Holy Bible mentions many times the renewal of the covenant with God, as happened in the days of Moses (Ex 24:5-7), in the days of King Asa (2 Chr 15:12, 13), likewise in the days of King Hezekiah (2 Chr 29:10), and then in the days of Ezra the priest (Ezra 10:30). This shows that the people of God turned back from their covenant with God many times, and God was longsuffering toward them, until Christ came and secured the covenant by His blood and gave us salvation in His Church through the Holy Sacraments.

10.2.1.en: Here we see Nehemiah's concern that the spiritual leaders and the leaders of the people should seal the covenant, so that they would be responsible for leading the people in holding fast to the covenant.

10.2.2.en: When you make any spiritual vows before God, be assured that this gladdens the heart of God. So take care on every occasion in your life to offer vows to God in order to live with Him, and let them be definite vows, and may you follow them up at intervals, such as every day and every week.

10.3.s.en: (2) Those who pledged themselves and the terms of the covenant

10.3.0.en: All classes of the people agreed to this covenant, which the priests, the Levites and the leaders sealed, that they might hold fast to everything in the covenant. Men and women took part in this agreement, and also the children, together with all those who worked in the Temple. The agreement of the children shows us the importance of caring for them. Therefore the Church in the New Testament has taken care to bring children into the covenant of God through the sacrament of Baptism under the care of their parents.

10.3.1.en: Those who agreed were not only the Jews, but those who had joined them from the Gentiles, and this is a type of God's receiving the Gentiles into the New Covenant together with the Jews.

10.3.2.en: This covenant was between two parties: the first party is God, and the second party is the people, represented by Nehemiah, the priests, the Levites and the leaders, followed by all the people in their different classes.

10.3.3.en: All classes of the people took part in this covenant, because all had sinned; therefore all should pledge themselves to a new life with God.

10.3.4.en: It says, “they that had separated themselves from the people of the lands ... every one having knowledge, and having understanding,” that is, those who had come of age and had mental understanding and acceptance of the Law of God. What is meant by those having knowledge and understanding may be those whose hearts were opened to know God, so they believed and understood and joined the people of God. Those who joined from the peoples of the lands declared their faith by word of mouth, by oath and swearing, and perhaps also by raising the hand. This oath and swearing means obtaining God's blessings if they held fast to the terms of the covenant, and their deserving of a curse when they broke the covenant. And their oath was to keep all the commandments.

10.3.5.en: Moses is called here the servant of God because of his great standing and his belonging to God, for he was faithful in his life with God and his service to Him.

10.4.0.en: The covenant included seven terms. The first was not to intermarry with the idolatrous peoples surrounding the people of God in the whole world, as the Law prescribed (Deut 7:3-4). The people of God were exposed to falling into this sin from the days of Moses and Joshua, and even after their return from the captivity they fell into this sin. It is a hard sin, because it leads to the worship of idols, and because of its seriousness it is mentioned as the first of the terms of the covenant. The believer's love for all people does not mean that he is lax toward sin and intermarries with unbelievers; rather he must hold fast to his faith and his spiritual teachings with all exactness.

10.4.1.en: The second term is keeping the Sabbath day, as God said (Ex 23:10-11, Lev 25:2). It is a holy day for the worship of God every week, on which no work is done, and therefore trading with the Gentiles on it is refused. The gates of Jerusalem and the Jewish cities were closed on it to prevent trade with foreigners. By this the believer declares his holding fast to the worship of God and refuses the material gain that would hinder him on the day of the Lord.

10.4.2.en: The third term in the covenant is the sanctification of the holy days, that is, the feasts and the spiritual seasons, and also the seventh year, the sabbath of the years, as God commanded them (Lev 26:34, 35), in which the Jews set free their brothers who had been enslaved to them and waived the debts owed to them by their brothers.

10.5.0.en: The fourth term in the covenant was the obligation of every man who reached the age of twenty years (Ex 30:13-14) to pay for the service of the Temple a third of a shekel of silver (Ex 30:16). A third of a shekel equals about 4 grams of silver. The Law required the man to pay half a shekel, but because of the hard economic circumstances through which the people of God were passing, since they were slaves and the goods of the land were taken by the king, they neglected payment to the Temple. Here they returned and offered a third of a shekel yearly, because of their extreme poverty. Nehemiah the governor did not compel the people to pay a sum to the Temple, but they bound themselves, out of their love for God. This sum was paid by the poor like the rich, to declare that the worth of each one is equal before God. Despite the smallness of the offering, because it came from all the people it sufficed for the needs of the Temple and its servants, such as the cost of the daily burnt offerings and the sacrifices offered at the seasons, and so on.

10.5.1.en: It is understood implicitly that there was no money in the Temple; the treasury was empty, and there was no Jewish king to help the Temple from his own funds, so the need was pressing that the people should pay a contribution to the Temple as the Law indicated. A similar situation had happened in ancient times in the days of King Joash, who encouraged the people to pay the contribution to the Temple and used the silver collected in restoring the Temple and organizing its service (2 Chr 24:

10.6.0.en: The group of the Nethinim, who were a company of Gentiles who joined the people of God in the days of Joshua, had as their service the gathering of wood for the service of the Temple. But only a small number of them returned from the captivity, not enough to gather the wood required for the Temple, so the people considered how to arrange and gather the wood, and agreed that it should fall on families of the priests, the Levites and the people, and that these families should be chosen by lot, to receive the blessing of this service. This was the fifth term of the covenant, namely the offering of the wood.

10.7.0.en: The sixth term of the covenant is the people's obligation to offer the firstfruits of their crops, whether plants or trees, and the firstfruits of the dough, and the firstborn of the animals, and also the firstborn of the sons of the people, or to offer silver for them to the Temple (Ex 13:2; Num 3:46). All these firstborn were offered to the priests.

10.7.1.en: Thus the people feel that God takes the firstborn of everything to bless the rest, and so they feel the hand of God with them. And the beautiful thing is that they commit themselves to all this despite their poverty, for giving out of want has great value before God, and of course God enriches them and blesses them more than they gave.

10.8.0.en: The seventh term in the covenant is the obligation to offer the tithes to the Levites, who in turn tithe what they have received, giving the tenth to the priests. Thus the storehouses of the Temple are filled with gifts, to be food for the priests and all who work in the Temple.

10.8.1.en: Offering tithes and firstfruits to God is love, in response to His love, which began and continues with us, for it is He who redeemed us and gave us His life and still takes care of us. May we always thank Him and express our love for Him, so that we gladden His heart and our hearts rejoice with Him.

11.0.0.en: It mentions the classes that dwelt in Jerusalem, which it will mention in detail in the following verses. In Jerusalem dwelt the rulers of the land, and also those chosen by lot from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, in addition to those chosen from the priests, the Levites, the Nethinim and the children of Solomon's servants, whose dwelling was necessary for the service of the Temple, so they dwelt beside it in Jerusalem. It does not give the details of the names and numbers of the children of Solomon's servants, who joined the people of God and helped in the service.

11.1.0.en: Of the children of Judah there dwelt four hundred and sixty-eight persons, all of them of the children of Pharez, from whose seed Christ came.

11.1.1.en: The number of the members of the tribe of Judah was less than that of the tribe of Benjamin, but they were men of valor, so they were suitable for guarding the city, as we heard of the seed of Judah from ancient times, “Judah is a lion's whelp” (Gen 49:9), that is, he is very strong.

11.2.0.en: Of the children of Benjamin there dwelt nine hundred and twenty-eight persons, a number greater than that of the tribe of Judah, because in Jerusalem Benjamin had a larger share than Judah.

11.2.1.en: It mentions an overseer of the Benjamites and an assistant to him, and this means that Nehemiah ordered them to organize their ranks for ease of governing them and guarding the city.

11.3.0.en: The priests were chosen from three houses, or clans, to dwell in Jerusalem, and the Holy Bible describes them as men of valor, distinguished in bodily strength, because the service of the priesthood, especially at the beginning of the restoration of the Temple, required no little effort.

11.3.1.en: The number of the priests was one thousand one hundred and ninety-two priests, which is a large number, and this shows the concern of the priests to return from the captivity for the service of the Temple, and they dwelt beside it in Jerusalem.

11.4.0.en: The number of the Levites was two hundred and forty-two, a small number compared with the priests, because some of them lived in the various lands to carry out the service of teaching the people the worship of God and the keeping of His commandments. It mentions that two of the Levites were responsible for the outward work of the Temple, such as collecting contributions or the materials needed for the service of the Temple, or teaching the people.

11.4.1.en: It also mentions two who were responsible for praise, and they were of the seed of the chief of the singers, Asaph and Jeduthun. This shows the concern in the Temple for praise and prayers, which must be joined with thanksgiving. It mentions that the number of the gatekeepers was one hundred and seventy-two, and this shows the concern for guarding the Temple, apart from the guarding of the city of Jerusalem.

11.4.2.en: We notice that it speaks of the people of God and calls them Israel, for the second time in this chapter (v. 3), because when the people of God returned from the captivity they were one unit, and the division that existed in ancient times before the captivity, namely the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah, was gone; after the captivity they became one kingdom called Israel, including all the tribes, Judah among them.

11.4.3.en: The Nethinim helped in the service of the Temple. They were the seed of the Gibeonites, of the Gentiles and not of the Jews, and they had joined the people of God in the days of Joshua. They dwelt in special dwellings in Ophel, which is a hill beside the wall of Jerusalem, at the Water Gate, to make their work easy for them, which was bringing water for the needs of the Temple.

11.5.0.en: The Levites had a chief and an overseer for them, who dwelt in Jerusalem and took care of managing the affairs of the Levites dwelling in Jerusalem or outside it, and they referred to him in every counsel. He was distinguished in leadership although he was one of the singers, but because of his administrative excellence he became the overseer of all the Levites.

11.5.1.en: The singers had been working for King Artaxerxes in the Persian capital, and when they came with Nehemiah, the king ordered that they should receive their allowances from the king while they were in Jerusalem, in return for offering supplications and prayers for him before the house of the Lord.

11.6.0.en: The Persian king Artaxerxes appointed an agent for himself in Jerusalem to collect the taxes, pay out of them what the Temple needed, and send the rest to the royal palace. It was a beautiful providence of God that the king chose this agent from the Jews, so that he would be compassionate toward them and not exploit them or steal from these funds for himself. All the numbers mentioned here of the Jews amount to two thousand six hundred and thirty-eight, apart from the leaders and the children of Solomon's servants, and also the Jews who had been in Jerusalem before Nehemiah. Although this number was small, God blessed them, so the city was rebuilt and multiplied within 400 years until Christ became incarnate, when the city was full of inhabitants.

11.6.1.en: How beautiful is the repopulating of the holy city, and better than it is the filling of the Church with worshipers. So take care to attend church regularly and encourage your loved ones, that all may receive a blessing and gladden the heart of God.

11.7.s.en: (3) The dwelling places of Judah and Benjamin outside Jerusalem

11.7.0.en: It tells us about the towns in which the tribe of Judah dwelt in Judea, that is, around Jerusalem. They were mentioned before in (Josh 15).

11.8.0.en: It mentions here the towns in which the tribe of Benjamin dwelt outside Jerusalem.

11.9.0.en: It points out to us here that the tribes of Judah and Benjamin took care to set apart places for the Levites to dwell among them, as Joshua the son of Nun commanded, and by this they carry out their role in teaching the people and guiding them.

11.9.1.en: Give a place of your time and attention to listening to the teachings of God from the mouth of the priests and deacons, and you will receive a blessing and walk in the way of the Kingdom.

11.9.2.en: The priesthood and the dedication of the wall. The book of Nehemiah presents to us the building of the wall of Jerusalem and how the resistance of the wicked was overcome, then tells us of the religious reform through the reading of the book of the Law, then the renewal of the covenant with God, and after this tells us of the dedication of the wall. But it did not fix the date of the dedication of the wall: was it done at the end of the twelve years that Nehemiah spent in Jerusalem, before his return to Shushan, the palace, the capital of the empire, or before this?

11.9.3.en: And in this chapter, before explaining to us how the wall was dedicated, it tells us of the list of the priests and Levites who came with Zerubbabel and down to the days of the dedication of the wall, because of the importance of the role of the priests and Levites in worship and dedication.
